newsitem.title: FRANCE: German gold plan turns spotlight on EMU questions.
newsitem.headline: German gold plan turns spotlight on EMU questions.

text.p: Germany's announcement about plans to revalue its gold reserves to bolster its finances has turned the spotlight onto a host of single currency issues, raising questions about deficits across the EU and lifting a taboo on the use of gold.

Economists said it was hard to comment in detail on the implication for Maastricht treaty criteria, since it was still unclear whether any extra resources generated would be used to cut Germany's deficit or reduce its debt.

But they said if Germany, which has led a drive for a strict interpretation of Maastricht treaty criteria, were to use the gold revaluation to cut its deficit this would undermine its hardline stance and make it all the easier for countries like Italy to argue their way into monetary union in 1999.
"If Germany were to use accounting tricks, it will not help them to keep Italy out," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.

Germany is seen as the most reluctant to allow Italy, which has imposed a special euro tax to meet Maastricht treaty criteria this year, to join the new euro from 1999, saying one-off measures are not acceptable to gain entry to EMU.

The German Bundesbank also harshly criticised a decision by France to use pension fund money from state-owned France Telecom to reduce its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year to meet Maastricht treaty criteria.

French officials declined comment on the German plans, though sources noted it was up to Germany to make its own decisions about its public finances and to EU authorities to decide whether these conformed with EU rules.

European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that he could not comment on the German plan until details were known, but said no "tricks" would be allowed.

Officials said that the plan to revalue German gold to reflect market prices did not in itself have immediate implications for European central banks, most of which, unlike Germany, already regularly revalue their reserves.

But economists said even raising the question of gold opened the door to a discussion -- which Germany has long resisted -- on how to use national central bank gold reserves which could be in surplus after they are pooled under monetary union.

Highlighting its concern about gold, the Bundesbank fiercely resisted a plan by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to sell some of its gold reserves to help finance a debt relief scheme for poor nations.
Diplomats said this resistance was driven in part by a desire not to set a precedent for Economic and Monetary Union.
Economists say European central banks may well have excess reserves after 1999 given that they will no longer need to defend national currencies after the launch of the euro.
"It seems to me that the aggregate gold reserves are beyond what they need," Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at Banque Internationale de Placement (BIP) in Paris, said.
She noted that countries like Belgium had already begun selling some of its gold reserves.

"Part of it is just a natural evolution in the modernisation of central banks. Gold has traditionally been an inflation hedge. If you don't think inflation is going to be a problem in the near future, there is much less reason to hold gold," she said.

France's Socialist party, campaigning in a parliamentary election, has suggested these excess gold reserves should be used to guarantee EU borrowing to finance a major programme of public works to boost growth and employment.
Such an idea would likely be anathema to the Bundesbank.
